Vagrancy is the state of wandering from place to place with no home and no job or money to live on.

For something to be vagrancy, all three of these need to be true:
🏠 no home + 🚶 keeps moving + 💰 no means of support

Say it VAY-gruhn-see, with the stress on the first syllable.
The trick is that vagrant rhymes with fragrant, and vagrancy sounds like fragrance with a V at the start and a -y on the end.
Don't say "vag-RAN-see."

The word comes from Latin vagari, "to wander." You already know some of its relatives:

  • vague: an idea that wanders and never settles on a clear point
  • extravagant: spending that wanders outside (extra) sensible limits
  • vagabond: an old, slightly romantic word for a wanderer
  • vagus nerve: the "wandering nerve," which travels all through your body

A vague idea has no fixed point. A person in vagrancy has no fixed home. Once you know that vag means wander, the word will stay with you.

It's America in 1932, during the Great Depression. A young man jumps off a freight train in a town he's never seen before. He has no money, no work and nowhere to sleep. A sheriff asks him where he lives and what he does. He has no answer, so he's arrested for vagrancy.

That one scene contains the whole word: wandering, no home, no work, and the law treating it as a crime.

• Homelessness just means having no home. It's the neutral, kind, modern word. A homeless person may stay in one city and even have a job.
  • Vagrancy means drifting with no home and no support. It sounds legal, historical or judgmental.

So when you talk about real people today, "homelessness" is usually the better word. Use "vagrancy" when you're talking about laws, history, courts, or the wandering itself.

• Vagrancy is the condition and has no plural in normal use. Vagrant is the person.
    ✗ He is a vagrancy. ✓ He is a vagrant. ✓ He was arrested for vagrancy.
  • Calling a real person "a vagrant" can sound insulting, so be careful with it.
6. Common word partners (learn them as chunks)

• arrested for / charged with vagrancy
  • vagrancy laws / anti-vagrancy laws
  • a life of / years of vagrancy
  • drift into / fall into vagrancy
  • poverty and vagrancy

• "In the 1800s, you could be jailed simply for vagrancy."
  • "After losing his job and his family, he slowly drifted into vagrancy."
  • "Those old vagrancy laws punished people for being poor, not for doing anything wrong."

• In literature: "the vagrancy of his thoughts" means a wandering mind. This use is rare and poetic.
  • In birdwatching: vagrancy is when a bird turns up far outside its normal area. It has wandered off course.
